name: Benfotiamine
summary: Benfotiamine is a fat-soluble, lab-made form of vitamin B1 (thiamin). It is sold as a supplement and has been studied mainly in diabetes-related nerve problems.
commonUses: May protect collagen in skin and other tissues from glycation, a sugar-related stiffening.
May reduce the formation of advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), harmful compounds made when sugar binds to proteins.
May improve skin firmness and elasticity.
May lower inflammation caused by high-glucose or high-protein diets.
roles: Once absorbed it supplies thiamin, which the body needs for energy metabolism. Whether extra thiamin from benfotiamine slows glycation or ageing is not established.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

examples: Not found in food (thiamin, vitamin B1, is found in whole grains, pork and pulses)

reference.noUpperLimit: No tolerable upper intake level has been set for benfotiamine. EFSA's 2026 novel-food opinion could not conclude that up to 300 mg a day is safe. No upper level was found for thiamin itself in the searches made for this guide.

cautions: Most human trials are in people with diabetes, using higher doses than many labels; results may not apply to healthy people.
In 2026 EFSA could not establish the safety of benfotiamine as a novel food, so it should not be assumed to have EU approval for that use.
Numbness, tingling or nerve pain need a doctor's assessment; a supplement is not a treatment for diabetes complications.
People who take regular medicines or are pregnant should check with a pharmacist or doctor first; no specific interaction was verified here.

origin: Benfotiamine is a lab-made, fat-soluble form of thiamin (vitamin B1). It does not occur in food. A related compound, allithiamine, is found in garlic and onion, but it is a different substance. After it is swallowed the body turns benfotiamine into thiamin and thiamin diphosphate, the active form.
It has been used mostly in studies of people with diabetes and nerve damage (neuropathy). Plain thiamin comes from whole grains, pork, legumes and seeds, and is added to many cereals.
dosage: There is no reference intake for benfotiamine. For thiamin itself, EFSA's 2016 opinion set a population reference intake of 0.1 mg per megajoule (0.4 mg per 1,000 kcal) for adults. In 2026 the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) assessed benfotiamine as a novel food for supplements for adults at up to 300 mg a day and could not conclude it is safe, citing unclear identity (including possible nanoparticles), manufacturing consistency, and limited data on metabolic fate and long-term effects. It judged that thiamin from benfotiamine may be better absorbed than from water-soluble forms, but did not quantify how much.

An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 150 to 300 mg a day (diabetic nerve trials used 300 to 600 mg a day, and some studies up to 900 mg). This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

When reading a label, check whether the form is benfotiamine or plain thiamin and how many milligrams it gives. Many products also contain other B vitamins. Because of the 2026 EFSA opinion, benfotiamine's status as a supplement ingredient in the EU may change; check the product's legal basis.
